passages.happening: “Do not rebuke an older man, but appeal to him as to a father. Treat younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, and younger women as sisters, with absolute purity” (verses 1-2).
passages.hearers:
Paul has called the church ‘God's household’ (3:15). Now he shows what that means for how a young leader treats people.

Timothy had to correct people, some of them older than he was. Paul does not tell him to stop correcting. He tells him how. An older man is to be approached as you would approach your own father: with respect, appealing to him, not scolding him. Younger men are brothers. Older women are mothers. Younger women are sisters.

In a world with sharp lines of rank, age and status, Paul turns the church into one family. Everyone has a place, and everyone is owed the love you would give your own kin.

And notice the last words: ‘with absolute purity’. A young leader dealing with younger women must be beyond reproach. Treating them as sisters means treating them with the honour and safety that a good brother would give. There is no room for anything else.
passages.ot:
Honouring the old is part of the law: “You are to rise in the presence of the elderly, honor the aged, and fear your God” (Leviticus 19:32). And honouring parents is one of the Ten Commandments: “Honor your father and mother” (Exodus 20:12).

The Old Testament shows what it looks like when someone treats another as true family, in Ruth's words to her mother-in-law: “your people will be my people, and your God will be my God” (Ruth 1:16).
passages.asks: Paul asks Timothy to treat every person in the church as family. Ask whom in your church you treat as a stranger rather than a brother, sister, father or mother. Ask how you speak to people older than you when you disagree. And ask whether everyone, especially the young and the vulnerable, is safe with you.

passages.t: Honour widows who are truly in need
passages.happening:
“Honor the widows who are truly widows. But if a widow has children or grandchildren, they must first learn to show godliness to their own family and repay their parents, for this is pleasing in the sight of God” (verses 3-4).

“The widow who is truly in need and left all alone puts her hope in God and continues night and day in her petitions and prayers. But she who lives for pleasure is dead even while she is still alive” (verses 5-6).

“If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially his own household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
In Paul's world a widow's life depended on her family. Her dowry was usually meant to support her if her husband died, and her children or her own birth family were expected to take her in. A widow with no family and no money could be left with nothing.

Care for widows was a mark of the faith of Israel, and the first church in Jerusalem gave food to its widows every day (Acts 6:1). By the time of this letter, the church in Ephesus seems to have had a list of widows it supported.

‘Honor’ here includes practical support, as it does in the command to honour your parents. Paul wants the church's help to go to those who truly need it: the widow ‘left all alone’. So families must care for their own first. That is simple godliness, and a way to ‘repay’ parents for what they gave. Even people outside the church expected children to care for widowed parents. A believer who did not would be ‘worse than an unbeliever’.

The widow ‘truly in need’ is also pictured as a woman of prayer, like Anna in the temple (Luke 2:36-37). The church's care frees her for that.
passages.ot: God's care for widows runs through the law and the prophets. “A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows, is God in His holy habitation” (Psalm 68:5). The law set aside food for them: “the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow within your gates may come and eat and be satisfied” (Deuteronomy 14:29). And the prophets demanded justice for them: “Defend the fatherless and plead the case of the widow” (Isaiah 1:17).
passages.hard:
Does ‘worse than an unbeliever’ mean that someone who cannot support their family has denied the faith?

No. Paul is speaking of people who could care for their widowed mothers and grandmothers and would not, leaving the church to carry what they could carry themselves. He is not speaking of people who are poor, sick, out of work or unable to help. The whole passage is about making sure that those truly in need are cared for.

The verse is a call to love your own family in practical ways. It is never a reason to shame someone who is struggling, and it is never a reason for a church to turn away someone in need.
passages.asks: Paul asks families to care for their own, so that the church can care for those who have no one. Ask whether there is an older relative who needs your help. Ask whether your church knows who is truly alone. And ask whether you honour your parents in ways that cost you something.

passages.t: The list of widows, and the younger widows
passages.happening:
“A widow should be enrolled if she is at least sixty years old, the wife of one man, and well known for good deeds such as bringing up children, entertaining strangers, washing the feet of the saints, imparting relief to the afflicted, and devoting herself to every good work” (verses 9-10).

But Paul says not to enroll younger widows, for they will want to marry, and some have become idle, ‘going from house to house’ as ‘gossips and busybodies’ (verses 11-13). “So I advise the younger widows to marry, have children, and manage their households, denying the adversary occasion for slander. For some have already turned aside to follow Satan” (verses 14-15).

A believing woman with widows in her family should help them, so that the church can help those truly in need (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
The church seems to have kept a list of widows it supported, and the women on it appear to have taken on a work of prayer and service. Their qualifications look like the lists for overseers and deacons in chapter 3: a record of good deeds, faithfulness, hospitality and care for others.

‘Washing the feet of the saints’ was the humble work of welcoming guests. Roads were dusty, and washing a guest's feet was a servant's task. Jesus did it for his disciples (John 13).

Why not enroll younger widows? It seems the enrolled widows made some kind of pledge to serve the church. Paul expects that younger women would, naturally and rightly, want to marry again, and then would break that pledge. He also reports a real problem: some younger widows had become idle and were spreading gossip, perhaps even the false teaching. Remember that the false teachers forbade marriage (4:3). Paul's answer is the opposite: let them marry.

In that world widows of an age to have children were usually expected to marry again, and Roman law under Augustus had encouraged them to. Paul's advice fits the life most widows then had.
passages.ot:
The good deeds Paul lists are the deeds of the woman of strength in Proverbs: “She opens her arms to the poor and reaches out her hands to the needy” (Proverbs 31:20).

And God sustains the widow: “The LORD protects foreigners; He sustains the fatherless and the widow” (Psalm 146:9). The law protected her from being exploited: “do not take a widow’s cloak as security” (Deuteronomy 24:17).
passages.hard:
Is Paul being hard on young women? Does verse 14 mean every young widow must remarry?

Modern readers can find these verses harsh, as though Paul distrusted young women. The setting softens that without removing the difficulty. The enrolled widows seem to have pledged themselves to the church's service, and Paul worries that younger women who later wished to marry would break that pledge. He also reports a real problem in Ephesus, of idleness, gossip and some following the false teachers. Marriage, which the false teachers forbade, is his remedy, not a punishment.

Elsewhere Paul says that a widow is free to marry again, and in his judgment happier if she stays as she is (1 Corinthians 7:39-40). So he did not think remarriage was required in every case. Most readers take verse 14 as practical counsel for a particular situation, not a law for every widow. A widow who chooses not to remarry, or who cannot, has done nothing wrong.

If you have lost a husband or a wife, the church is meant to be family to you. Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul's list of widows honours women who spent their lives caring for others. Ask whom in your church you could honour for years of quiet service. Ask whether your words build others up, or move from house to house as gossip. And ask whether there is someone grieving the loss of a spouse whom you could stand beside.

passages.t: Honour good elders; weigh accusations fairly
passages.happening:
“Elders who lead effectively are worthy of double honor, especially those who work hard at preaching and teaching” (verse 17). Paul backs this with two sayings he calls Scripture: ‘Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain’, and ‘The worker is worthy of his wages’ (verse 18).

“Do not entertain an accusation against an elder, except on the testimony of two or three witnesses. But those who persist in sin should be rebuked in front of everyone, so that the others will stand in fear of sin” (verses 19-20).

“I solemnly charge you before God and Christ Jesus and the elect angels to maintain these principles without bias, and to do nothing out of partiality. Do not be too quick in the laying on of hands and thereby share in the sins of others. Keep yourself pure” (verses 21-22).
passages.hearers:
‘Double honor’ seems to include both respect and pay. Paul backs it with two sayings he calls Scripture. One is from the law of Moses: an ox treading out grain should be allowed to eat as it works. The other matches the words of Jesus, ‘the worker is worthy of his wages’ (Luke 10:7). It is striking that a saying of Jesus stands beside the law under the name ‘Scripture’.

Then Paul turns to elders accused of wrong. The rule of ‘two or three witnesses’ comes from the law. A leader is a public target, and one angry or careless person could ruin him with a rumour. So an accusation needs to be tested.

But Paul at once guards the other side. An elder who ‘persists in sin’ is not protected by his office. He is to be rebuked ‘in front of everyone’, because a leader's sin harms many. And Paul puts the most solemn charge in the letter on it: before God, Christ Jesus and the angels, do this ‘without bias’, with nothing done ‘out of partiality’. No favourites. No protecting a friend.

Finally, do not be ‘too quick’ to lay hands on someone, that is, to appoint a new leader. Take time to know their life. Rushing to appoint someone makes you share the blame for what follows.
passages.ot:
Paul quotes the law: “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain” (Deuteronomy 25:4). The priests and Levites were paid for their work too: “it is the compensation for your work at the Tent of Meeting” (Numbers 18:31).

The rule of witnesses is the law's: “A matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deuteronomy 19:15). The law also forbade favouritism in judging: “you must not show partiality to the poor or favoritism to the rich; you are to judge your neighbor fairly” (Leviticus 19:15). And it forbade siding with the crowd against the truth: “When you testify in a lawsuit, do not pervert justice by siding with the crowd” (Exodus 23:2).
passages.hard:
Does verse 19 mean that a report of abuse by a church leader should be ignored unless there are two or three witnesses?

No. Paul's rule protects leaders from being ruined by gossip or a single grudge, and that is right. But the same passage says that a leader who persists in sin must be rebuked in front of everyone, and that it must all be done without bias or favouritism. Paul does not let anyone protect a leader because of his position.

Abuse is very often done where there are no other witnesses. Verse 19 is about how a church weighs an accusation in its own discipline. It is never a reason to dismiss a report, to keep it quiet, or to ask a person who has been harmed to stay silent.

This passage, like others about discipline, has also been badly misused, and that must be faced. Church discipline must never be used to silence someone who has been harmed, to protect someone who has done harm, or to punish someone for asking questions or telling the truth. Abuse and other crimes are reported to the police and the proper authorities, whom Paul calls “God’s servant, an agent of retribution to the wrongdoer” (Romans 13:4). A church meeting is never a substitute for that.

A word to anyone who has been hurt by a church's discipline, or shunned by a church or a family. What happened to you may have been wrong, and it is not wrong to grieve it. Paul's goal was always restoration and comfort, never cruelty or contempt. “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted” (Psalm 34:18). If this still weighs on you, please talk with someone you trust, a pastor, a friend or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul asks the church to honour good leaders, protect them from gossip, and still hold them to account without favouritism. Ask whether you honour those who serve you well, in words and in practical ways. Ask whether you have ever passed on an accusation you had not tested. And ask whether you would protect a leader you liked even when he was wrong.

passages.t: A little wine, and what cannot stay hidden
passages.happening:
“Stop drinking only water and use a little wine instead, because of your stomach and your frequent ailments” (verse 23).

“The sins of some men are obvious, going ahead of them to judgment; but the sins of others do not surface until later. In the same way, good deeds are obvious, and even the ones that are inconspicuous cannot remain hidden” (verses 24-25).
passages.hearers:
Verse 23 is a small, personal note in the middle of serious instructions. Timothy was often unwell. Ancient medicine used wine for stomach troubles and other ailments, and drinking water was often unsafe. Timothy may have been drinking only water as a kind of self-denial. If so, Paul's advice fits his answer to the false teachers in chapter 4, who made refusing God's gifts a mark of holiness. Paul cares about Timothy's body.

Then Paul returns to the choosing of leaders, and gives a word of comfort and warning. Some people's sins are plain to see. Others come out only later. The same is true of good deeds: some are obvious, and even the quiet ones will come to light. So take time before appointing someone. And trust that God sees what people miss, both the hidden wrong and the hidden good.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament speaks of wine both as a gift and as a danger. It is “wine that gladdens the heart of man” (Psalm 104:15). It is also “a mocker, strong drink is a brawler, and whoever is led astray by them is not wise” (Proverbs 20:1). Some in Israel, the Rechabites, kept away from it all their lives (Jeremiah 35:6).

And nothing stays hidden from God: “For God will bring every deed into judgment, along with every hidden thing, whether good or evil” (Ecclesiastes 12:14). “He who conceals his sins will not prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them will find mercy” (Proverbs 28:13).
passages.hard:
Does verse 23 mean that Christians should drink wine, or that they may?

Paul's words are advice to one man about his health, not a rule for anyone else. Christians agree that drunkenness is sin, that no one should be pressured to drink, that people harmed by alcohol and people caught in it need care, and that believers should not despise one another over a matter Scripture leaves to conscience (Romans 14). Beyond that they differ, and these notes do not choose.

Many Baptist, Methodist, Holiness and Pentecostal churches have long taught or encouraged abstaining from alcohol altogether. They point to its power to harm and enslave, the warnings of Proverbs, and the call in Romans 14 to give up a freedom for the sake of others. Many other Christians, among them Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican and Reformed churches, hold that drinking in moderation is a lawful use of God's gift. They point to Psalm 104, the wedding at Cana and wine at the Lord's Supper, while warning just as seriously against drunkenness. Both take the danger seriously, and both honour the gift of a clear mind. These notes are not medical advice.

If drinking has become hard to control, you do not have to face it alone. Tell someone you trust, and reach out to a doctor or a recovery group near you. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul cared for Timothy's health, and reminded him that God sees what is hidden. Ask whether you look after your body as a gift, or treat it as unimportant. Ask whether there is a hidden sin you need to bring into the light before it comes out on its own. And take heart if your good work is unseen: it cannot stay hidden from God.
